Which ordination and which test? Advice from the data and the question

Source: R/ordination-advise.R
ord_advise.Rd

ord_advise() helps choose an ordination method and the test that goes with it. It looks at the community data (number of sites and species, zeros, abundances or presence-absence, the length of the main gradient) and at the question asked, and recommends, with its reasons and the code to run:

  • unconstrained or constrained. To describe the main patterns of composition, without a hypothesis about their causes, use an unconstrained (indirect) ordination: PCA, CA or NMDS; site variables can be fitted afterwards (arrows, contours) but are not part of the analysis. To test whether, and how much, measured variables explain composition, use a constrained (direct, canonical) ordination: RDA, CCA or distance-based RDA, with a permutation test.

  • linear or unimodal. The length of the first axis of a detrended correspondence analysis, in standard-deviation units of species turnover, measures how heterogeneous the data are: below about 3, most species change monotonically and linear methods (PCA, RDA) fit; above about 4, species rise and fall along the gradient and unimodal methods (CA, CCA) fit; in between, either (ter Braak and Smilauer 2012). Hellinger-transformed PCA and RDA (Legendre and Gallagher 2001) work well whatever the length, and NMDS or distance-based RDA with Bray-Curtis or Jaccard dissimilarity suit any data.

  • the test. Constrained ordinations are tested by permutation (overall, by axis and by term); with many candidate variables, by forward selection; differences between groups of sites by PERMANOVA, with a test of dispersion alongside; treatments followed over time by principal response curves; and the separate and shared effects of sets of variables by variation partitioning.

The advice is a starting point, not a rule: the question, which only the analyst knows, comes first.

Usage

ord_advise(
  data,
  site = site,
  species = species,
  abundance = NULL,
  formula = NULL,
  question = c("auto", "explore", "explain", "groups", "time", "partition"),
  treatment = NULL,
  time = NULL
)

Arguments

data

A data frame in long format, with one row per record.

site, species

<tidy-select> The column holding site identifiers and the column holding species names.

abundance

<tidy-select> The column holding counts. If NULL (the default), a column called abundance is used when present, otherwise every row counts as one individual.

formula

Optional one-sided formula of site variables (columns of data, one value per site), e.g. ~ elevation + habitat.

question

What is asked: "auto" (from the other arguments), "explore" (describe the main patterns), "explain" (test site variables), "groups" (compare groups of sites), "time" (treatments followed over time) or "partition" (separate the effects of sets of variables).

treatment, time

Optional columns for a treatment followed over time.

Value

A list of class td_ord_advice: checks (a tibble of what was measured in the data, its value and what it means), advice (a tibble of steps: step, recommendation, reason and code) and gradient_length. Printing it shows the advice.

References

ter Braak, C. J. F. and Smilauer, P. (2012). Canoco Reference Manual and User's Guide: Software for Ordination (version 5.0). Microcomputer Power.

Legendre, P. and Gallagher, E. D. (2001). Ecologically meaningful transformations for ordination of species data. Oecologia, 129, 271-280.

Legendre, P. and Legendre, L. (2012). Numerical Ecology, third edition. Elsevier.

Examples

data("dune", "dune.env", package = "vegan")
d <- community_long(cbind(site = rownames(dune), dune.env, dune),
  cols = dplyr::all_of(names(dune))
)
# Describe the meadows
ord_advise(d, abundance = abundance)
#> 
#> ── tidyvisor: which analysis? ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Question: explore
#> 
#> ── What the data show ──
#> 
#> • Sites: "20"
#> • Species: "30"
#> • Data: "abundances"
#> • Zeros: "67%" — many zeros: shared absences must not make sites similar
#>   (Hellinger or Bray-Curtis)
#> • Species in one site only: "10%"
#> • Gradient length (DCA axis 1, SD units): "3.52" — intermediate: linear or
#>   unimodal methods both suit
#> • Site variables (model terms): "0"
#> 
#> ── Recommended ──
#> 
#> Approach: Unconstrained (indirect) ordination
#> You want to describe the main patterns of composition, not test their causes.
#> Method: PCA on Hellinger-transformed data, or NMDS
#> Gradient length 3.5 SD; NMDS on bray dissimilarity suits any data.
#> ord_fit(data, abundance = abundance, method = "pca", transform = "hellinger")
#> ord_fit(data, abundance = abundance, method = "nmds", distance = "bray")
#> Interpret: Fit site variables afterwards (arrows, contours, centroids)
#> Fitted variables are a post hoc interpretation of the axes; their permutation
#> p-values are descriptive.
#> autoplot(ord, surface = <numeric variable>)
#> Check: Scree diagram (PCA, CA) or Shepard diagram and stress (NMDS)
#> How many axes are worth reading, and how faithful the diagram is.
#> autoplot(ord, type = "scree")   # or type = "shepard"
#> Plots: Biplot with numeric variables as contours or symbol size, factors as
#> centroids; scree or Shepard inset; stability ellipses
#> Contours show non-linear change that an arrow hides; the inset shows how
#> faithful the diagram is; ellipses show which sites are placed firmly.
#> autoplot(ord, surface = <numeric>, colour = <factor>, inset = "scree")   # "shepard" for NMDS
#> autoplot(ord, type = "gradient", path = <numeric>)
#> autoplot(ord, type = "stability")
#> Interpret: Plain-language explanation of the tables and the diagram
#> Variation explained, tests, directions of variables, groups, species at each
#> end of the axes, and how to read the plot.
#> ord_interpret(ord)
# Test management and soil
ord_advise(d, abundance = abundance, formula = ~ A1 + Moisture + Management)
#> 
#> ── tidyvisor: which analysis? ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Question: explain
#> 
#> ── What the data show ──
#> 
#> • Sites: "20"
#> • Species: "30"
#> • Data: "abundances"
#> • Zeros: "67%" — many zeros: shared absences must not make sites similar
#>   (Hellinger or Bray-Curtis)
#> • Species in one site only: "10%"
#> • Gradient length (DCA axis 1, SD units): "3.52" — intermediate: linear or
#>   unimodal methods both suit
#> • Site variables (model terms): "7" — many terms for the sites: select
#>   variables (forward selection)
#> 
#> ── Recommended ──
#> 
#> Approach: Constrained (direct, canonical) ordination
#> You have a hypothesis that measured site variables explain composition.
#> Method: RDA on Hellinger-transformed data (or db-RDA)
#> Gradient length 3.5 SD.
#> ord <- ord_fit(data, abundance = abundance, method = "rda", transform = "hellinger", formula = ~A1 + Moisture + Management)
#> Select: Forward selection of variables
#> Too many or collinear variables inflate the explained variation and make the
#> test unreliable.
#> ord_select(data, abundance = abundance, formula = ~A1 + Moisture + Management)
#> Test: Permutation tests: the whole model, each axis and each term
#> The F-test of a constrained ordination has no parametric distribution;
#> permuting sites gives p-values.
#> ord_test(ord, by = "model"); ord_test(ord, by = "axis"); ord_test(ord, by = "margin")
#> Plots: Triplot; species response curves along the main variable; t-value biplot
#> or Van Dobben circles
#> The triplot shows sites, species and variables together; response curves show
#> each species' optimum and tolerance with confidence bands; Van Dobben circles
#> single out the species that respond significantly.
#> autoplot(ord)
#> autoplot(ord, type = "response", variable = "<numeric>")
#> autoplot(ord, type = "vandobben", variable = "<numeric>")
#> Interpret: Plain-language explanation of the tables and the diagram
#> Variation explained, tests, directions of variables, groups, species at each
#> end of the axes, and how to read the plot.
#> ord_interpret(ord)
